subject: DI01000021

intro_text.en: Unit 2 of Mathematics-I: angles in degrees and radians with arc length, sector area and angular speed; the six trigonometric functions and the ASTC signs; allied angles; compound angles sin(A ± B), cos(A ± B) and tan(A ± B); multiple and submultiple (double, half and triple) angles; the graphs of sine and cosine with amplitude, period and phase; the sum and factor formulae in both directions; and inverse trigonometric functions with their principal ranges. Twenty-six fully solved numericals, every one linked to a card.

h.en: 1.1 Degree and radian measure

body.en:
Definition

An angle is the amount of rotation from an initial arm to a terminal arm. The two units of angles are the degree (one full turn = 360°) and the radian (one full turn = 2π); the same rotation gives the same angle in either unit.

The conversion

π radians = 180°, so radians = degrees × π/180 and degrees = radians × 180/π. One radian is about 57.3°.

Angles you should know instantly

Degrees0°30°45°60°90°180°360°
Radians0π/6π/4π/3π/2π2π

Why radians

A radian is defined by arc length: 1 radian subtends an arc equal to the radius. That is why arc length, sector area and angular speed formulas only work when θ is in radians - and why calculus in later semesters uses radians only.

h.en: 1.2 Arc length and area of a sector

body.en:
Formulae

For a circle of radius r and an angle θ in radians:

arc length s = rθ and sector area A = ½ r²θ.

Derivation

A full turn is 2π radians and its arc is the circumference 2πr. So a fraction θ/2π of the circle has arc (θ/2π)(2πr) = rθ. The full area is πr², so the same fraction gives (θ/2π)(πr²) = ½r²θ. Both formulas are proportions - nothing new is memorised.

Common mistake / conditions

Substituting degrees directly gives nonsense: for θ = 60° and r = 7, rθ = 420, which is far larger than the whole circumference. Convert to π/3 first, then s = 7π/3 ≈ 7.33 cm.

h.en: 1.3 Angular speed and linear speed

body.en:
Definition

Angular speed ω is the angle swept per second (rad/s); linear speed v is the distance travelled per second along the circle. They are linked by v = rω.

Conversions

  • 1 revolution = 2π radians, so rpm × 2π/60 gives rad/s.
  • 1 rad/s at radius r gives v = r m/s with r in metres.
  • Frequency f (revolutions per second) gives ω = 2πf.

Worked example

A wheel of radius 30 cm turns at 300 rpm. ω = 300 × 2π/60 = 10π ≈ 31.42 rad/s, so v = 0.30 × 31.42 ≈ 9.42 m/s. Doubling the radius doubles the rim speed at the same rpm - the reason a larger wheel covers more ground per turn.

h.en: 2.1 The six ratios, from triangle to unit circle

body.en:
Definition

In a right triangle, for an acute angle θ: sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan θ = opposite/adjacent, with cosec, sec and cot as their reciprocals.

The unit-circle definition

Take a point P(x, y) on the circle of radius 1 at angle θ from the positive x-axis. Then cos θ = x, sin θ = y and tan θ = y/x. This extends the ratios to every angle, including obtuse, negative and reflex angles, because x and y carry signs.

Signs are automatic here

A point in the second quadrant has x < 0, so cos θ < 0 there while sin θ > 0. You do not need a rule to remember - just picture the point.

h.en: 2.2 Signs in the four quadrants

body.en:
Definition

The ASTC rule (All, Sin, Tan, Cos) says which functions are positive in each quadrant, counting anticlockwise from the positive x-axis.

QuadrantAngle rangePositive functionsMemory line
I0° to 90°all sixAll
II90° to 180°sin and cosecSilver
III180° to 270°tan and cotTea
IV270° to 360°cos and secCups

Reading it from the circle

In Q II the x-coordinate is negative and y positive, so only sin (= y) is positive. In Q III both are negative, so their ratio tan is positive. In Q IV x is positive, so cos is positive.

Common mistake / conditions

tan θ is undefined at 90° and 270° (the point has x = 0, so y/x divides by zero), and cot θ, cosec θ, sec θ are undefined wherever their own denominators vanish. State the excluded angles when the question asks for the domain.

h.en: 2.3 The standard-angle table

body.en:
Definition

Five angles carry almost every numerical in this unit. Learn the table and you can evaluate any allied angle without a calculator.

θ0°30°45°60°90°
sin θ01/21/√2√3/21
cos θ1√3/21/√21/20
tan θ01/√31√3not defined

Pattern worth noticing

sin runs 0, 1/2, 1/√2, √3/2, 1 - the values are √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2. cos is the same list reversed, which is why sin 30° = cos 60°.

Conditions

tan 90° is undefined, not infinite; write "not defined" in an exam. The table is for exact values - use decimals only when a question asks for them.

h.en: 2.4 The three fundamental identities

body.en:
Identities

sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ, 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.

Where the first one comes from

On the unit circle P(x, y) has x² + y² = 1 by Pythagoras, and x = cos θ, y = sin θ. Divide that same equation by cos²θ and you get the second identity; divide by sin²θ and you get the third. One equation produces all three.

How they are used

To turn a sum into a single term: 1 − sin²θ = cos²θ; to simplify a fraction; and to find the third ratio from one given value plus a quadrant. Given sin θ = 3/5 with θ in Q II, cos²θ = 1 − 9/25 = 16/25, so cos θ = −4/5 (negative because the quadrant says so).

h.en: 3.1 The allied-angle rules

body.en:
Definition

Allied angles are built from θ using 180°, 360° and the negative sign. Two steps always work: decide the sign from the quadrant, then use θ itself as the angle.

Anglesincostan
−θ−sin θcos θ−tan θ
90° − θcos θsin θcot θ
90° + θcos θ−sin θ−cot θ
180° − θsin θ−cos θ−tan θ
180° + θ−sin θ−cos θtan θ
270° − θ−cos θ−sin θcot θ
360° − θ−sin θcos θ−tan θ

The rule in words

For odd multiples of 90° the function changes (sin ↔ cos); for even multiples it stays. The sign comes from the quadrant of the original angle. Example: sin(180° + θ) keeps the name sin, lies in Q III where sin is negative, so the answer is −sin θ.

h.en: 3.2 Evaluating large and negative angles

body.en:
Procedure

  1. Reduce the angle into 0°-360° by adding or subtracting 360° (the functions are periodic).
  2. Use the allied-angle rule to bring it into 0°-90°.
  3. Substitute the standard value.

Worked examples

sin 150° = sin(180° − 30°) = sin 30° = 1/2. cos 240° = cos(180° + 60°) = −cos 60° = −1/2. tan 315° = tan(360° − 45°) = −tan 45° = −1. sin(−330°) = −sin 330° = −(−1/2) = 1/2.

Common mistake / conditions

Do not drop the sign because the numbers look small: 240° is in Q III, so its cosine must be negative even though cos 60° = 1/2. Write the quadrant in the margin before evaluating.

h.en: 4.1 sin(A ± B) and cos(A ± B)

body.en:
Formulae

sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B, sin(A − B) = sin A cos B − cos A sin B

cos(A + B) = cos A cos B − sin A sin B, cos(A − B) = cos A cos B + sin A sin B

How the pattern is remembered

sin keeps the signs it is given; cos flips them. In sin the two terms are sine-cosine and cosine-sine; in cos the cosines come first in both terms.

Where it is used

It turns an unknown angle into two known ones: 75° = 45° + 30° and 15° = 45° − 30°. That is why sin 75° can be written exactly as (√6 + √2)/4 ≈ 0.966 without a calculator.

h.en: 4.2 tan(A ± B)

body.en:
Formula

tan(A + B) = (tan A + tan B)/(1 − tan A tan B) and tan(A − B) = (tan A − tan B)/(1 + tan A tan B).

Derivation (two lines)

Write tan(A + B) = sin(A + B)/cos(A + B), substitute the two formulas above, and divide numerator and denominator by cos A cos B. The result follows.

Worked example

tan 75° = tan(45° + 30°) = (1 + 1/√3)/(1 − 1/√3) = (√3 + 1)/(√3 − 1) = 2 + √3 ≈ 3.732 (rationalise by multiplying by (√3 + 1)/(√3 + 1), since (√3 − 1)(√3 + 1) = 2).

Conditions

The formula fails when a denominator is zero - for example tan(A + B) when A + B = 90°. Check the angle before substituting.

h.en: 4.3 Compound-angle numericals with given ratios

body.en:
Method

  1. Draw a right triangle (or use sin² + cos² = 1) to find the missing ratios.
  2. Fix each sign by the quadrant given in the question.
  3. Substitute into the compound-angle formula and simplify.

Worked example

If sin A = 3/5 and cos B = 5/13 with A, B acute, then cos A = 4/5 and sin B = 12/13. So sin(A + B) = (3/5)(5/13) + (4/5)(12/13) = 15/65 + 48/65 = 63/65 ≈ 0.969.

Why the check matters

A and B are acute, so A + B is between 0° and 180°; sin(A + B) must be positive, and 63/65 is. If you get a negative sine, a quadrant sign is wrong.

h.en: 4.4 Heights and distances: the engineering use

body.en:
Definition

Surveying, civil and mechanical work all reduce to one right triangle: a horizontal distance d, a vertical height h, and the angle of elevation (looking up) or depression (looking down).

The three relations

  • tan θ = h/d - the workhorse, because it links the two distances.
  • sin θ = h/L where L is the slant length (a ladder, a cable, a ramp).
  • cos θ = d/L - use it when the sloping length is the known quantity.

Worked example

From 50 m away the top of a tower is seen at 30° above the horizontal: h = 50 tan 30° = 50/√3 ≈ 28.87 m. If the angle were 45°, the height would equal the distance - the quickest sanity check in the field.

Conditions

Both angles are measured from the horizontal, and the instrument height is added to h. Sketch the triangle and mark the right angle before writing any ratio.

h.en: 5.1 Double-angle formulae

body.en:
Formulae

sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A; cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A;

tan 2A = 2 tan A / (1 − tan²A).

Derivation

Put B = A in the compound formulas: sin(A + A) = sin A cos A + cos A sin A = 2 sin A cos A, and cos(A + A) = cos²A − sin²A. Replacing sin²A by 1 − cos²A (or the reverse) gives the two other forms of cos 2A - choose the one that matches what the question gives you.

Worked example

sin A = 3/5 with A acute gives cos A = 4/5, so sin 2A = 2(3/5)(4/5) = 24/25 and cos 2A = 16/25 − 9/25 = 7/25.

h.en: 5.2 Submultiple (half-angle) formulae

body.en:
Formulae

From cos 2A = 1 − 2sin²A, with 2A replaced by θ: sin(θ/2) = ±√((1 − cos θ)/2);

cos(θ/2) = ±√((1 + cos θ)/2); tan(θ/2) = (1 − cos θ)/sin θ = sin θ/(1 + cos θ).

The sign question

The ± is decided by the quadrant of θ/2, not of θ. If θ = 300°, then θ/2 = 150° lies in Q II, where sine is positive and cosine negative - so the sine takes + and the cosine takes −.

Worked example

sin 15° = √((1 − cos 30°)/2) = √((1 − √3/2)/2) = √(2 − √3)/2 ≈ 0.2588, which agrees with sin(45° − 30°) computed by the compound formula.

h.en: 5.3 Triple-angle formulae

body.en:
Formulae

sin 3A = 3 sin A − 4 sin³A; cos 3A = 4 cos³A − 3 cos A;

tan 3A = (3 tan A − tan³A)/(1 − 3 tan²A).

Derivation

Write 3A = 2A + A and apply sin(A + B) with B = 2A, then substitute the double-angle results and replace cos²A by 1 − sin²A. Every multiple-angle formula is built this way.

Worked example

With sin A = 1/2: sin 3A = 3(1/2) − 4(1/8) = 1.5 − 0.5 = 1, and indeed 3A = 90° when A = 30°. The formula is a check on itself.

h.en: 6.1 Graphs of sin x and cos x

body.en:
Shape

Both curves oscillate between −1 and 1. sin x starts at 0 and rises; cos x starts at 1 and falls. They are the same wave shifted by 90°: cos x = sin(x + 90°).

Key points of one cycle

x0π/2π3π/22π
sin x010−10
cos x10−101

Words used with graphs

  • Amplitude: half the distance between maximum and minimum (1 for both curves).
  • Period: length of one complete cycle (2π for both).
  • Zeros: where the curve crosses the axis - sin at 0, π, 2π; cos at π/2, 3π/2.
  • Maximum / minimum: 1 and −1, reached once per cycle.

Sketching five points and joining them with a smooth wave is enough for an exam answer - a table of values plus the shape earns the marks.

h.en: 6.2 Periodic functions and the period of sin kx

body.en:
Definition

A function is periodic with period T if f(x + T) = f(x) for every x, and T is the smallest such positive number. sin x and cos x have period 2π; tan x has period π.

Changing the frequency

FunctionAmplitudePeriod
sin x, cos x12π
sin kx, cos kx12π/|k|
tan kxnoneπ/|k|
a sin kx|a|2π/|k|

Worked examples

sin 3x has period 2π/3, so three cycles fit in 0 to 2π. cos(x/2) has period 4π - it is slower, not faster. tan 2x has period π/2. A common error is dividing by k in the wrong direction; test with k = 2: the curve repeats twice as often, so the period must be halved.

h.en: 6.3 Reading y = a sin(bx + c) + d

body.en:
The four numbers

LetterNameWhat it does
aamplitudestretches vertically; range becomes d − |a| to d + |a|
bfrequencyperiod becomes 2π/|b|
cphaseshifts left by c/b (right if negative)
dvertical shiftmoves the whole graph up or down

Worked example

y = 3 sin(2x − π/3) + 1: amplitude 3, period π, phase shift π/6 to the right, centre line y = 1, so the range is −2 to 4 and the maximum 4 occurs when sin(...) = 1.

Conditions

The phase shift is c/b only when the bracket is written as b(x + c/b) - factor b out first. Without that step the shift is reported as c, which is the standard mistake.

h.en: 7.1 Sum and difference into product

body.en:
Formulae

sin C + sin D = 2 sin((C + D)/2) cos((C − D)/2)

sin C − sin D = 2 cos((C + D)/2) sin((C − D)/2)

cos C + cos D = 2 cos((C + D)/2) cos((C − D)/2)

cos C − cos D = −2 sin((C + D)/2) sin((C − D)/2) - note the leading minus.

Derivation

Add the two compound formulas sin(A + B) and sin(A − B): the cosine terms cancel and 2 sin A cos B remains. Put A = (C + D)/2 and B = (C − D)/2 and the first formula appears. Subtracting instead of adding gives the second; the cosine pair works the same way.

Worked example

sin 75° + sin 15° = 2 sin 45° cos 30° = 2 × (√2/2)(√3/2) = √6/2 ≈ 1.225, which matches 0.966 + 0.259 = 1.225 ✓.

h.en: 7.2 Product into sum or difference

body.en:
Formulae

2 sin A cos B = sin(A + B) + sin(A − B)

2 cos A sin B = sin(A + B) − sin(A − B)

2 cos A cos B = cos(A + B) + cos(A − B)

2 sin A sin B = cos(A − B) − cos(A + B)

How to use them

These turn a product (hard to integrate later) into a sum. Choose the pair whose sum and difference are the angles you have: 2 sin 40° cos 20° = sin 60° + sin 20° ≈ 0.866 + 0.342 = 1.208.

Simplifications worth knowing

(sin A + sin 3A)/(cos A + cos 3A) = (2 sin 2A cos A)/(2 cos 2A cos A) = tan 2A. Questions of this type are always solved by converting every sum into a product and cancelling.

h.en: 8.1 Definition and principal values

body.en:
Definition

sin⁻¹x is the angle in a fixed principal range whose sine is x. The restriction makes the inverse a genuine function, because the original sine repeats.

FunctionDomainPrincipal range
sin⁻¹x−1 ≤ x ≤ 1−π/2 to π/2
cos⁻¹x−1 ≤ x ≤ 10 to π
tan⁻¹xall real x−π/2 to π/2
cot⁻¹xall real x0 to π

Notation warning

sin⁻¹x means arcsin x, not 1/sin x. The reciprocal is cosec x. Write arcsin x if the distinction matters.

Reading the ranges

cos⁻¹(−1/2) = 2π/3, not −π/3: −π/3 is outside the principal range 0 to π, and the inverse must return a value inside it.

h.en: 8.2 Compositions and the range trap

body.en:
Definition

sin⁻¹(sin x) = x only when x already lies in the principal range. Outside it, reduce the angle first.

Worked examples

sin⁻¹(sin 5π/6): 5π/6 = 150° is outside −90° to 90°, but sin 150° = sin 30°, so the answer is π/6, not 5π/6. By contrast sin(sin⁻¹ 0.4) = 0.4 always, because 0.4 is in the domain.

The complement identity

sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2 for every x in [−1, 1], and tan⁻¹x + cot⁻¹x = π/2. These follow from the cofunction relation sin(π/2 − θ) = cos θ.

Common mistake / conditions

Do not cancel sin⁻¹ and sin blindly. Ask first: is the angle inside the principal range? If not, use an allied angle to bring it in.

h.en: 8.3 Sum of two inverse tangents

body.en:
Formula

tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹y = tan⁻¹((x + y)/(1 − xy)) when xy < 1, and the answer shifts by π when xy > 1 (because the sum passes 90°).

Worked example

tan⁻¹1 + tan⁻¹2 + tan⁻¹3: first 1 and 2 give (3)/(1 − 2) = −3, an angle in Q II, so the pair sums to π − tan⁻¹3; adding tan⁻¹3 gives π. Numerically 45° + 63.43° + 71.57° = 180° ✓.

Why the condition matters

With x = y = 2 the fraction is 4/(1 − 4) = −4/3, a negative number, but both angles are positive and their sum is about 126.9°, which is π − tan⁻¹(4/3). Forgetting the π shift is the usual error in this question.

h.en: Practice 1. Convert 210° into radians and 3π/4 radians into degrees.

body.en:
Working

  1. 210 × π/180 = 7π/6
  2. 3π/4 × 180/π = 135°

Answer

7π/6 and 135°. 210° is 30° past 180°, so it must be a little more than π - and 7π/6 ≈ 1.17π ✓.

h.en: Practice 2. Find the arc length and sector area for r = 12 cm, θ = 45°.

body.en:
Working

  1. θ = π/4
  2. s = 12 × π/4 = 3π ≈ 9.42 cm
  3. A = ½ × 144 × π/4 = 18π ≈ 56.55 cm²

Check

The arc is one eighth of the circumference 2π(12) = 75.4 cm, and 75.4/8 = 9.42 ✓.

h.en: Practice 3. If cos θ = −5/13 and θ is in the third quadrant, find sin θ and tan θ.

body.en:
Working

  1. sin²θ = 1 − 25/169 = 144/169
  2. In Q III sine is negative: sin θ = −12/13
  3. tan θ = (−12/13)/(−5/13) = 12/5

Check

25/169 + 144/169 = 1 ✓, and tan is positive in Q III as ASTC predicts ✓.

h.en: Practice 4. Evaluate tan 120° and cos 315° without a calculator.

body.en:
Working

tan 120° = tan(180° − 60°) = −tan 60° = −√3. cos 315° = cos(360° − 45°) = cos 45° = 1/√2 = √2/2.

Answer

−√3 and √2/2. Q II gives tangent a negative sign; Q IV gives cosine a positive sign.

h.en: Practice 5. Find cos 105° exactly using a compound angle.
Practice 6. If tan A = 3/4 and A is acute, find sin 2A and cos 2A.

body.en:
Working

  1. sin A = 3/5, cos A = 4/5 (3-4-5 triangle)
  2. sin 2A = 2(3/5)(4/5) = 24/25
  3. cos 2A = 2(16/25) − 1 = 7/25

Check

(24/25)² + (7/25)² = 1 ✓. A ≈ 36.87°, so 2A ≈ 73.74° is still in Q I and both values are positive.

h.en: Practice 7. Find the period and amplitude of y = 5 cos(3x + π/4).

body.en:
Working

Amplitude = |5| = 5 and period = 2π/3; the phase shift is π/12 to the left because c/b = (π/4)/3.

Answer

Amplitude 5, period 2π/3. Range is −5 to 5, centre line y = 0.

h.en: Practice 8. Express cos 40° − cos 20° as a product.

body.en:
Working

  1. Use cos C − cos D = −2 sin((C + D)/2) sin((C − D)/2)
  2. = −2 sin 30° sin 10°
  3. = −2(1/2) sin 10° = −sin 10°

Check

Numerically: 0.766 − 0.940 = −0.174, and −sin 10° = −0.1736 ✓. The leading minus in the cosine formula is what makes the answer negative.

h.en: Practice 9. Simplify sin 5θ + sin 3θ over cos 5θ + cos 3θ.

body.en:
Working

  1. Numerator: 2 sin 4θ cos θ
  2. Denominator: 2 cos 4θ cos θ
  3. Ratio = tan 4θ

Answer

tan 4θ. The cos θ cancels for every θ where it is not zero, which is why the identity holds wherever the original expression is defined.

h.en: Practice 10. Evaluate sin⁻¹(−1/2), cos⁻¹(1/2) and tan⁻¹(−1).

body.en:
Working

sin⁻¹(−1/2) = −π/6 (principal range −π/2 to π/2). cos⁻¹(1/2) = π/3. tan⁻¹(−1) = −π/4.

Answer

−π/6, π/3, −π/4. Odd inverse functions keep the sign of the input; the cosine inverse does not, because its range starts at 0.

h.en: Practice 11. Find the principal value of cos⁻¹(cos 7π/6).

body.en:
Working

  1. cos 7π/6 = cos 210° = −√3/2
  2. cos⁻¹(−√3/2) = 5π/6
  3. So the answer is 5π/6, not 7π/6

Check

cos 5π/6 = −√3/2 ✓ and 5π/6 lies in [0, π] ✓. 7π/6 is outside the principal range, which is exactly why it cannot be the answer.

h.en: Practice 12. A ladder makes 60° with the ground and reaches 6 m up a wall. How far is its foot from the wall?

body.en:
Working

  1. tan 60° = 6/d
  2. d = 6/tan 60° = 6/√3
  3. d = 2√3 ≈ 3.46 m

Check

The ladder length is 6/sin 60° = 6.93 m, and 3.46² + 6² = 48 = 6.93² ✓.

h.en: Practice 13. Solve 2 sin²θ − 1 = 0 for 0° ≤ θ ≤ 360°.

body.en:
Working

  1. sin²θ = 1/2, so sin θ = ±1/√2
  2. sin θ = +1/√2 → θ = 45°, 135°
  3. sin θ = −1/√2 → θ = 225°, 315°

Answer

θ = 45°, 135°, 225°, 315°. Four solutions are expected because sine takes each value twice per full turn.

h.en: Practice 14. Find sin 22.5° using a half-angle formula.

body.en:
Working

  1. 22.5° = 45°/2
  2. sin(θ/2) = √((1 − cos θ)/2) = √((1 − √2/2)/2)
  3. = √((2 − √2)/4) = √(2 − √2)/2

Check

√(2 − √2)/2 ≈ 0.3827, which is sin 22.5° as a calculator confirms. The positive root is correct because 22.5° lies in Q I.

h.en: Practice 15. Prove that sin 2A/(1 + cos 2A) = tan A.

body.en:
Working

Left side = 2 sin A cos A / (2cos²A), using sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A and 1 + cos 2A = 2cos²A. Cancel 2 cos A: = sin A/cos A = tan A.

Check

Test A = 30°: left = sin 60/(1 + cos 60) = 0.866/1.5 = 0.577 and tan 30° = 0.577 ✓. Choosing the form 1 + cos 2A = 2cos²A is what makes the proof work.

q.en: Convert 135° into radians and 5π/6 radians into degrees.

a.en:
Given and assumptions

Use π radians = 180°.

Formula

radians = degrees × π/180; degrees = radians × 180/π

Step-by-step solution

  1. 135 × π/180 = 3π/4
  2. 5π/6 × 180/π = 150

Interpretation and check

3π/4 and 150°. Check the first: 135° is three quarters of 180°, so three quarters of π ✓. A radian answer larger than 2π for an angle under 360° is always wrong.

q.en: Find the arc length and the sector area for r = 7 cm and θ = 60°.

a.en:
Given and assumptions

θ must be in radians before either formula is used: 60° = π/3.

Formula

s = rθ and A = ½r²θ

Step-by-step solution

  1. θ = π/3 ≈ 1.0472 rad
  2. s = 7 × 1.0472 = 7.33 cm
  3. A = ½ × 49 × 1.0472 = 25.66 cm²

Interpretation and check

s ≈ 7.33 cm, A ≈ 25.66 cm². Check the arc: it is one sixth of the circumference 2π(7) = 43.98, and 43.98/6 = 7.33 ✓.

q.en: A wheel of radius 30 cm rotates at 300 rpm. Find its angular speed and the linear speed of a point on the rim.

a.en:
Given and assumptions

300 revolutions per minute; radius 0.30 m.

Formula

ω = rpm × 2π/60 rad/s; v = rω

Step-by-step solution

  1. ω = 300 × 2π/60 = 10π ≈ 31.42 rad/s
  2. v = 0.30 × 31.42 = 9.42 m/s

Interpretation and check

ω ≈ 31.42 rad/s, v ≈ 9.42 m/s. Sanity: 5 revolutions per second means the rim travels 5 × 2π(0.30) = 9.42 m each second ✓.

q.en: If sin θ = 3/5 and θ lies in the second quadrant, find cos θ and tan θ.

a.en:
Given and assumptions

θ in Q II: sine positive, cosine and tangent negative.

Formula

sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 and tan θ = sin θ / cos θ

Step-by-step solution

  1. cos²θ = 1 − 9/25 = 16/25
  2. cos θ = −4/5 because Q II makes cosine negative
  3. tan θ = (3/5)/(−4/5) = −3/4

Interpretation and check

cos θ = −4/5, tan θ = −3/4. Check the identity: 9/25 + 16/25 = 1 ✓. The quadrant decides the signs; without it the answer is ambiguous.

q.en: Evaluate sin 30° cos 60° + cos 30° sin 60°.

a.en:
Given and assumptions

This is exactly the expansion of sin(A + B) with A = 30°, B = 60°.

Formula

sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B

Step-by-step solution

  1. Recognise the pattern: sin(30° + 60°) = sin 90°
  2. = 1
  3. Direct check: (1/2)(1/2) + (√3/2)(√3/2) = 1/4 + 3/4 = 1

Interpretation and check

1. Recognising the pattern is faster and safer than multiplying decimals. Both routes must agree - a mismatch means a wrong standard value.

q.en: Evaluate sin²30° + cos²60° + tan²45°.

a.en:
Given and assumptions

Standard values only; no identity needed, but the first identity can be used as a check.

Formula

sin 30° = 1/2, cos 60° = 1/2, tan 45° = 1

Step-by-step solution

  1. (1/2)² = 1/4
  2. (1/2)² = 1/4
  3. 1² = 1
  4. 1/4 + 1/4 + 1 = 3/2

Interpretation and check

3/2 = 1.5. Notice sin²30° + cos²60° = 1/2 only because both angles give 1/2; in general sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 uses the same angle.

q.en: Write sin(180° + θ), cos(180° − θ) and tan(360° − θ) in terms of θ.

a.en:
Given and assumptions

Use the quadrant sign plus the unchanged function name (even multiple of 90°).

Formula

Sign from the quadrant; name stays for 180° and 360°

Step-by-step solution

  1. 180° + θ is in Q III, sine negative → sin(180° + θ) = −sin θ
  2. 180° − θ is in Q II, cosine negative → cos(180° − θ) = −cos θ
  3. 360° − θ is in Q IV, tangent negative → tan(360° − θ) = −tan θ

Interpretation and check

−sin θ, −cos θ and −tan θ. Test with θ = 30°: sin 210° = −0.5 ✓, cos 150° = −0.866 ✓, tan 330° = −0.577 ✓.

q.en: Evaluate sin 150°, cos 240°, tan 315° and sin(−330°).

a.en:
Given and assumptions

Reduce each angle with an allied-angle rule first.

Formula

sin(180° − θ) = sin θ, cos(180° + θ) = −cos θ, tan(360° − θ) = −tan θ, sin(−θ) = −sin θ

Step-by-step solution

  1. sin 150° = sin 30° = 1/2
  2. cos 240° = −cos 60° = −1/2
  3. tan 315° = −tan 45° = −1
  4. sin(−330°) = −sin 330° = −(−1/2) = 1/2

Interpretation and check

1/2, −1/2, −1 and 1/2. Each answer matches the ASTC sign of its quadrant: Q II sine positive, Q III cosine negative, Q IV tangent negative, and −330° is coterminal with 30°.

q.en: Find sin 75° exactly.

a.en:
Given and assumptions

75° = 45° + 30°, both standard angles.

Formula

sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B

Step-by-step solution

  1. = sin 45 cos 30 + cos 45 sin 30
  2. = (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2)
  3. = (√6 + √2)/4

Interpretation and check

(√6 + √2)/4 ≈ 0.9659. 75° is close to 90°, so its sine should be close to 1 - and 0.966 is. A calculator gives 0.96593 ✓.

q.en: Find cos 15° exactly.

a.en:
Given and assumptions

15° = 45° − 30°.

Formula

cos(A − B) = cos A cos B + sin A sin B

Step-by-step solution

  1. = cos 45 cos 30 + sin 45 sin 30
  2. = (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2)
  3. = (√6 + √2)/4

Interpretation and check

(√6 + √2)/4 ≈ 0.9659. This is the same value as sin 75°, which is expected because 15° and 75° are complementary: cos 15° = sin 75° ✓.

q.en: Find tan 75° in surd form.

a.en:
Given and assumptions

75° = 45° + 30°.

Formula

tan(A + B) = (tan A + tan B)/(1 − tan A tan B)

Step-by-step solution

  1. = (1 + 1/√3)/(1 − 1/√3)
  2. Multiply top and bottom by √3: (√3 + 1)/(√3 − 1)
  3. Rationalise: ((√3 + 1)²)/((√3)² − 1²) = (4 + 2√3)/2 = 2 + √3

Interpretation and check

2 + √3 ≈ 3.732. Check: tan 75° must exceed tan 60° = 1.732 ✓, and 2 + 1.732 = 3.732 matches a calculator.

q.en: If sin A = 3/5 and cos B = 5/13 with A and B acute, find sin(A + B).

a.en:
Given and assumptions

Acute angles, so every ratio is positive.

Formula

sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B

Step-by-step solution

  1. cos A = √(1 − 9/25) = 4/5
  2. sin B = √(1 − 25/169) = 12/13
  3. sin(A + B) = (3/5)(5/13) + (4/5)(12/13)
  4. = 15/65 + 48/65 = 63/65

Interpretation and check

63/65 ≈ 0.969. Both angles are acute so A + B < 180° and the sine is positive ✓. The Pythagorean triples 3-4-5 and 5-12-13 make the arithmetic exact.

q.en: If sin A = 3/5 with A acute, find sin 2A and cos 2A.

a.en:
Given and assumptions

cos A = 4/5 from the same triangle.

Formula

sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A; cos 2A = 1 − 2 sin²A

Step-by-step solution

  1. sin 2A = 2(3/5)(4/5) = 24/25
  2. cos 2A = 1 − 2(9/25) = 7/25

Interpretation and check

24/25 and 7/25. Check with the identity: (24/25)² + (7/25)² = (576 + 49)/625 = 1 ✓. Since A ≈ 36.87°, 2A ≈ 73.74° lies in Q I, so both values must be positive.

q.en: Find cos 2A when cos A = 1/2.

a.en:
Given and assumptions

Choose the form of cos 2A that uses cos A only.

Formula

cos 2A = 2 cos²A − 1

Step-by-step solution

  1. = 2(1/4) − 1
  2. = 1/2 − 1 = −1/2

Interpretation and check

−1/2. A = 60°, so 2A = 120° and cos 120° = −1/2 ✓. Choosing the wrong form (1 − 2sin²A) would need sin A first - extra work, same answer.

q.en: Find sin 15° using a half-angle formula.

a.en:
Given and assumptions

15° = 30°/2, so use θ = 30° with the positive root (15° is in Q I).

Formula

sin(θ/2) = √((1 − cos θ)/2)

Step-by-step solution

  1. = √((1 − √3/2)/2)
  2. = √((2 − √3)/4)
  3. = √(2 − √3)/2

Interpretation and check

√(2 − √3)/2 ≈ 0.2588. Check against the compound formula: sin(45° − 30°) = (√6 − √2)/4 ≈ 0.2588 ✓. The two surd forms are equal.

q.en: Using the triple-angle formula, evaluate sin 3A when sin A = 1/2 and A is acute.

a.en:
Given and assumptions

A = 30°, so 3A = 90°; the formula must reproduce sin 90° = 1.

Formula

sin 3A = 3 sin A − 4 sin³A

Step-by-step solution

  1. = 3(1/2) − 4(1/8)
  2. = 1.5 − 0.5
  3. = 1

Interpretation and check

1. The known value of sin 90° confirms the formula. This is a useful exam habit: when a formula can be checked against a standard angle, do it.

q.en: Find the period of sin 3x, cos(x/2) and tan 2x.

a.en:
Given and assumptions

Period of sin kx and cos kx is 2π/|k|; of tan kx it is π/|k|.

Formula

T = 2π/|k| for sine and cosine, T = π/|k| for tangent

Step-by-step solution

  1. sin 3x: T = 2π/3
  2. cos(x/2): k = 1/2, T = 2π/(1/2) = 4π
  3. tan 2x: T = π/2

Interpretation and check

2π/3, 4π and π/2. Sanity: the larger the k, the faster the oscillation and the smaller the period - sin 3x repeats three times in 2π, so its period is one third of 2π ✓.

q.en: For y = 3 sin(2x − π/3) state the amplitude, period, phase shift and range.

a.en:
Given and assumptions

Compare with y = a sin(bx + c) + d: a = 3, b = 2, c = −π/3, d = 0.

Formula

amplitude |a|, period 2π/|b|, shift −c/b, range d ± |a|

Step-by-step solution

  1. Amplitude = 3
  2. Period = 2π/2 = π
  3. Shift = π/6 to the right
  4. Range = −3 to 3

Interpretation and check

3, π, π/6 right, [−3, 3]. Check one extreme: the maximum 3 occurs when 2x − π/3 = π/2, that is x = 5π/12, inside the first period ✓.

q.en: Find the maximum and minimum of y = 2 + 3 cos x.

a.en:
Given and assumptions

cos x varies between −1 and 1.

Formula

y = d + a cos x has range d ± |a|

Step-by-step solution

  1. Maximum when cos x = 1: y = 2 + 3 = 5
  2. Minimum when cos x = −1: y = 2 − 3 = −1

Interpretation and check

Maximum 5, minimum −1. The centre line is y = 2 and the amplitude 3, so the range is 2 ± 3 ✓. The maxima occur at x = 0, 2π, … and the minima at x = π, 3π, ….

q.en: Express sin 75° + sin 15° as a product and evaluate it.

a.en:
Given and assumptions

C = 75°, D = 15°, so (C + D)/2 = 45° and (C − D)/2 = 30°.

Formula

sin C + sin D = 2 sin((C + D)/2) cos((C − D)/2)

Step-by-step solution

  1. = 2 sin 45° cos 30°
  2. = 2 × (√2/2) × (√3/2)
  3. = √6/2

Interpretation and check

√6/2 ≈ 1.2247. Direct check: 0.9659 + 0.2588 = 1.2247 ✓. The product form also shows why the sum exceeds 1 even though each term is below 1.

q.en: Convert 2 sin 40° cos 20° into a sum and evaluate it.

a.en:
Given and assumptions

A = 40°, B = 20° in the product-to-sum formula.

Formula

2 sin A cos B = sin(A + B) + sin(A − B)

Step-by-step solution

  1. = sin 60° + sin 20°
  2. = 0.8660 + 0.3420
  3. = 1.2080

Interpretation and check

sin 60° + sin 20° ≈ 1.208. Check the product directly: 2(0.6428)(0.9397) = 1.208 ✓.

q.en: Simplify (sin A + sin 3A)/(cos A + cos 3A).

a.en:
Given and assumptions

Convert both sums to products; the common factor should cancel.

Formula

sin C + sin D = 2 sin((C + D)/2) cos((C − D)/2); cos C + cos D = 2 cos((C + D)/2) cos((C − D)/2)

Step-by-step solution

  1. Numerator: 2 sin 2A cos(−A) = 2 sin 2A cos A
  2. Denominator: 2 cos 2A cos(−A) = 2 cos 2A cos A
  3. Ratio = tan 2A

Interpretation and check

tan 2A. Check with A = 20°: numerator = sin 20 + sin 60 = 0.342 + 0.866 = 1.208, denominator = cos 20 + cos 60 = 0.940 + 0.500 = 1.440, ratio = 0.839 = tan 40° ✓.

q.en: Evaluate sin⁻¹(1/2), cos⁻¹(−1/2) and tan⁻¹(1).

a.en:
Given and assumptions

Use the principal ranges: sin⁻¹ in [−π/2, π/2], cos⁻¹ in [0, π], tan⁻¹ in (−π/2, π/2).

Formula

y = sin⁻¹x ⇔ sin y = x within the principal range

Step-by-step solution

  1. sin 30° = 1/2 → sin⁻¹(1/2) = π/6
  2. cos 120° = −1/2 → cos⁻¹(−1/2) = 2π/3
  3. tan 45° = 1 → tan⁻¹(1) = π/4

Interpretation and check

π/6, 2π/3 and π/4. The trap is cos⁻¹(−1/2): −π/3 has the right cosine but lies outside 0 to π, so it is not the principal value.

q.en: Evaluate sin⁻¹(sin 5π/6).

a.en:
Given and assumptions

5π/6 = 150° is outside the principal range [−90°, 90°].

Formula

sin⁻¹(sin x) = x only when x is inside the principal range

Step-by-step solution

  1. sin 150° = sin 30° = 1/2
  2. sin⁻¹(1/2) = π/6
  3. Therefore sin⁻¹(sin 5π/6) = π/6

Interpretation and check

π/6, not 5π/6. Check: sin π/6 = 1/2 = sin 5π/6 ✓, and π/6 is inside the principal range. This question exists to test exactly that restriction.

q.en: Show that tan⁻¹1 + tan⁻¹2 + tan⁻¹3 = π.

a.en:
Given and assumptions

Combine the first two with the addition formula, then add the third.

Formula

tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹y = tan⁻¹((x + y)/(1 − xy)) with a π shift when xy > 1

Step-by-step solution

  1. For 1 and 2: (1 + 2)/(1 − 2) = −3, and xy = 2 > 1, so the sum is π − tan⁻¹3
  2. Add tan⁻¹3: π − tan⁻¹3 + tan⁻¹3 = π

Interpretation and check

π. Numerically 45° + 63.43° + 71.57° = 180° ✓. Without the π shift the algebra gives tan⁻¹(−3) + tan⁻¹3 = 0, which is clearly wrong for a sum of three positive angles.

q.en: The angle of elevation of the top of a tower is 30° from a point 50 m from its base. Find the height of the tower.

a.en:
Given and assumptions

Right triangle: adjacent = 50 m, angle = 30°, opposite = height h.

Formula

tan θ = opposite / adjacent

Step-by-step solution

  1. tan 30° = h/50
  2. h = 50 × tan 30° = 50/√3
  3. h = 50√3/3 ≈ 28.87 m

Interpretation and check

h ≈ 28.87 m. Sanity: tan 30° ≈ 0.577, so the height is a little more than half the distance ✓. Rationalise the surd: 50/√3 = 50√3/3.

q.en: How many radians make 180°?

a.en: π radians, so 1 radian ≈ 57.3°.

q.en: Write the arc-length formula and state the unit of θ.

a.en: s = rθ, with θ in radians.

q.en: Write the sector-area formula.

a.en: A = ½r²θ, with θ in radians.

q.en: How do you convert rpm into rad/s?

a.en: Multiply by 2π/60, because one revolution is 2π radians in 60 seconds.

q.en: State the ASTC rule.

a.en: Quadrant I all positive, II sin positive, III tan positive, IV cos positive.

q.en: Which functions are positive in the third quadrant?

a.en: tan θ and cot θ only, because both coordinates are negative and their ratio is positive.

q.en: Give the three fundamental identities.

a.en: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ, 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.

q.en: Write sin(180° − θ).

a.en: sin θ: the angle is in Q II where sine is positive, and the name stays.

q.en: Write cos(180° + θ).

a.en: −cos θ: Q III makes cosine negative.

q.en: State sin(A + B).

a.en: sin A cos B + cos A sin B.

q.en: State cos(A − B).

a.en: cos A cos B + sin A sin B - the cosine formula flips the sign.

q.en: State tan(A + B).

a.en: (tan A + tan B)/(1 − tan A tan B).

q.en: Why is sin 75° equal to sin 45° cos 30° + cos 45° sin 30°?

a.en: Because 75° = 45° + 30° and the compound-angle formula expands sin(A + B).

q.en: State sin 2A.

a.en: 2 sin A cos A.

q.en: Give the three forms of cos 2A.

a.en: cos²A − sin²A, 2cos²A − 1 and 1 − 2sin²A.

q.en: State sin 3A.

a.en: 3 sin A − 4 sin³A.

q.en: What is the period of sin 3x?

a.en: 2π/3, because the frequency is 3.

q.en: What is the amplitude of y = 3 sin(2x − π/3)?

a.en: 3, the magnitude of the coefficient of the sine.

q.en: Write sin C + sin D as a product.
Write 2 sin A cos B as a sum.

a.en: sin(A + B) + sin(A − B).

q.en: What is the principal range of sin⁻¹?

a.en: −π/2 to π/2, inclusive.

q.en: What is sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x?

a.en: π/2 for every x in [−1, 1].

Practice: If cos θ = −5/13 and θ is in the third quadrant, find sin θ and tan θ.
Practice: Evaluate tan 120° and cos 315° without a calculator.
Practice: Find cos 105° exactly using a compound angle.
Practice: If tan A = 3/4 and A is acute, find sin 2A and cos 2A.
Practice: Find the period and amplitude of y = 5 cos(3x + π/4).
Practice: Express cos 40° − cos 20° as a product.
Practice: Simplify sin 5θ + sin 3θ over cos 5θ + cos 3θ.
Practice: Evaluate sin⁻¹(−1/2), cos⁻¹(1/2) and tan⁻¹(−1).
Practice: Find the principal value of cos⁻¹(cos 7π/6).
Practice: A ladder makes 60° with the ground and reaches 6 m up a wall. How far is its foot from the wall?
Practice: Solve 2 sin²θ − 1 = 0 for 0° ≤ θ ≤ 360°.
Practice: Find sin 22.5° using a half-angle formula.
Practice: Prove that sin 2A/(1 + cos 2A) = tan A.
